introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0765 Pure Maths with Mechanics 1, June 2022, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL questions; each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D and only one answer must be marked (if more than one answer is marked the score for that question is zero). Formulae booklets and calculators are allowed. Section A: Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35); Section B: Mechanics (questions 36 to 50). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.

figures.legende: Figure 1 (Q41): uniform L-shaped metal sheet; vertical left edge AB of length 6 (B at the top, A at the bottom), upright arm 2 wide, foot 6 long and 2 high.

Figure 2 (Q42): ladder AB against a vertical wall on the left (B at the top) and the floor (A at the bottom right, angle theta with the floor); forces 6 N up and 9 N horizontal at B, weight 42 N at the middle, 36 N up and 9 N horizontal at A.

Question 17 (convertie en ouverte) : la fonction imprimée est f(x) = sin(2x/3), de période 3 pi, valeur absente des quatre options (4pi/3, 2pi/3, 3pi/4, 3pi/2). La bonne valeur n'est dans aucune option.

Question 20 (convertie en ouverte) : les options A et C sont imprimées de façon identique (i - 2j - k). La bonne réponse, i - 2j + k (option B), est unique mais le défaut d'impression rend la question non fiable pour une correction automatique.

Question 42 (convertie en ouverte) : les fractions des options sont surimprimées et illisibles ; les options C et D se lisent toutes deux sin(theta) = 3/5. La bonne réponse, tan(theta) = 5/3 (option B), est unique et obtenue par les moments en A à partir des forces lues sur la Fig. 2 (6 N et 9 N en B, poids 42 N, 36 N et 9 N en A).
Question 46 (convertie en ouverte) : avec F = i - 2j - 4k, r_A = 3i - 4k et r_B = -i + 6k (relus à fort grossissement), le travail vaut -44 J, valeur absente des options (47, -35, -15, 35).

Question 19 : la lettre y à gauche de la seconde équation paramétrique (« [y] = 1/cos theta ») n'est pas lisible dans le scan ; elle est restituée entre crochets dans l'énoncé et le corrigé. Avec y = 1/cos theta, la réponse C (x^2 - y^2 - 2x + 2 = 0) est la seule valable.

Avec k au numérateur, la somme vaut 2k = 10 donc k = 5 (option B, présente dans les options). Sans k, la série imprimée vaut 2 et la question n'aurait pas de sens.

Question 37 : la valeur de g n'est pas imprimée dans cette question ; g = 10 m/s2 est retenue (valeur imposée aux questions 47 et 48) et donne 5 racine de 3 m, option C ; avec g = 9,8 on obtiendrait 8,84 m, qui ne figure dans aucune option.

Question 41 : les cotes de la Fig. 1 (6 le long du bord vertical AB, 2 de largeur du bras vertical, 6 de longueur du pied, 2 de hauteur du pied) sont lues sur la figure, qui n'est pas à l'échelle ; la distance du centre de masse à AB est 2,2 m (option A). L'arête AB est lue comme le bord vertical gauche (B en haut, A en bas) ; par symétrie du L, la distance à l'arête horizontale du bas serait la même.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

The remainder when the polynomial $f(x)=2x^3+ax^2-3x+1$ is divided by $(x+1)$ is $-2$. The value of the constant $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: By the remainder theorem the remainder on division by $(x+1)$ is $f(-1)$. $f(-1)=2(-1)^3+a(-1)^2-3(-1)+1=-2+a+3+1=a+2$. Setting $a+2=-2$ gives $a=-4$. Option B ($4$) comes from a sign slip, and option C ($-5$) from forgetting the term $-3(-1)=+3$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the roots of the equation $2x^2+5x-3=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$, then the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For $2x^2+5x-3=0$: $\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac{5}{2}$ and $\alpha\beta=-\dfrac{3}{2}$. Then $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta=\dfrac{25}{4}+3=\dfrac{37}{4}$. Check: the roots are $\tfrac12$ and $-3$, and $\tfrac14+9=\tfrac{37}{4}$. Option C is $(\alpha+\beta)^2$ alone; options A and D come from a wrong multiple of $\alpha\beta$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\dfrac{x+1}{(x-3)(x-5)}\equiv\dfrac{M}{x-3}+\dfrac{N}{x-5}$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply by $(x-3)(x-5)$: $x+1\equiv M(x-5)+N(x-3)$. Put $x=3$: $4=M(-2)$, so $M=-2$. Put $x=5$: $6=N(2)$, so $N=3$. Check: $-2(x-5)+3(x-3)=x+1$. The wrong options come from dropping the sign of $x-5$ when $x=3$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution set of the inequality $|2x-1|>3$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $|2x-1|>3$ means $2x-1>3$ or $2x-1<-3$. The first gives $x>2$, the second gives $x<-1$. So the solution set is $\{x:x<-1\ \text{or}\ x>2\}$. Option C is the solution of $|2x-1|<3$ (the values between the two boundary points), and B and D result from mishandling the constant $-1$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A partial order relation is that which is
questions.corrige_markdown: By definition, a partial order on a set is a relation that is reflexive, anti-symmetric and transitive (for example $\le$ on $\mathbb R$ or $\subseteq$ on sets). Option A describes an equivalence relation (symmetric instead of anti-symmetric), B omits transitivity, and D omits reflexivity. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of distinct arrangements of the letters of the word ABRACADABRAR is
questions.corrige_markdown: The word ABRACADABRAR has $12$ letters: A appears $5$ times, B appears $2$ times, R appears $3$ times, and C and D once each ($5+2+3+1+1=12$). The number of distinct arrangements is $\dfrac{12!}{5!\,2!\,3!}$, which is the expression in option A (the order of the factors in the denominator does not matter). Options B, C and D use a wrong number of repeated B's or R's. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is given by $f(x)=ax+b$. If $f(3)=3$ and $f(4)=5$, then the values of the constants $a$ and $b$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: $f(3)=3a+b=3$ and $f(4)=4a+b=5$. Subtracting the first from the second gives $a=2$, and then $b=3-6=-3$. Check: $f(3)=6-3=3$ and $f(4)=8-3=5$. Option A has the wrong sign of $b$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $2\log_4 8$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\log_4 8=\dfrac{\ln 8}{\ln 4}=\dfrac{3\ln 2}{2\ln 2}=\dfrac32$ (equivalently $4^{3/2}=8$). So $2\log_4 8=2\times\dfrac32=3$. Option B is $\log_4 8$ without the factor $2$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $u_n=5+\dfrac32(n-1)$ is the $n^{\text{th}}$ term of an arithmetic progression, the sum of the first twenty terms of the progression is
questions.corrige_markdown: The first term is $a=u_1=5$ and the common difference is $d=\dfrac32$. The sum of the first $n$ terms is $S_n=\dfrac n2\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$, so $S_{20}=10\left[10+19\times\dfrac32\right]=10(10+28.5)=385$. Option A ($770$) is double this value (it forgets the factor $\tfrac12$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{(1-x)(x-3)}{(x+2)}>0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The critical values are $x=-2$ (where the denominator vanishes), $x=1$ and $x=3$ (zeros of the numerator). Here $(1-x)(x-3)=-(x-1)(x-3)$, which is positive for $1<x<3$ and negative outside $[1,3]$, while $x+2$ is positive for $x>-2$. Sign table: for $x<-2$ the numerator is negative and the denominator negative, so the quotient is positive; for $-2<x<1$ the quotient is negative; for $1<x<3$ it is positive; for $x>3$ it is negative. Checks: $x=-3$ gives $\dfrac{(4)(-6)}{(-1)}=24>0$; $x=0$ gives $\dfrac{(1)(-3)}{2}<0$; $x=2$ gives $\dfrac{(-1)(-1)}{4}>0$; $x=4$ gives $\dfrac{(-3)(1)}{6}<0$. So the solution set is $\{x:x<-2\}\cup\{x:1<x<3\}$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $p$ and $q$ are two statements. The compound statement $p\Rightarrow q$ is false when
questions.corrige_markdown: The truth table of $p\Rightarrow q$ shows that it is false only in the single case where $p$ is true and $q$ is false (a true hypothesis cannot lead to a false conclusion). When both statements are false the implication is true, and equal truth values never make it false. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value
$p$ and $q$ are converse of each other

questions.enonce_markdown: If $a+bi=\dfrac{1+i}{1-2i}$, the values of the constants $a$ and $b$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $1+2i$: $\dfrac{(1+i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}=\dfrac{1+2i+i+2i^2}{1+4}=\dfrac{-1+3i}{5}$. So $a=-\dfrac15$ and $b=\dfrac35$. Check: $(1-2i)\left(-\dfrac15+\dfrac35 i\right)=-\dfrac15+\dfrac35 i+\dfrac25 i-\dfrac65 i^2=1+i$. The other options come from the sign error $i^2=+1$ or from conjugating wrongly. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $x^2-4x+9\equiv(x+A)^2+B$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Complete the square: $x^2-4x+9=(x-2)^2-4+9=(x-2)^2+5$. Comparing with $(x+A)^2+B$ gives $A=-2$ and $B=5$. Check: $(x-2)^2+5=x^2-4x+9$. Options A and B take $A=+2$ (wrong sign), and options A and C take $B=3$ (a slip in $-4+9$). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two variables $y$ and $x$ are connected by the equation $y=a(x+2)^k$. A linear equivalence of this equation is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take logarithms of both sides: $\log y=\log a+\log (x+2)^k=k\log(x+2)+\log a$. This is of the form $Y=mX+c$ with $Y=\log y$, $X=\log(x+2)$, gradient $k$ and intercept $\log a$. In option A the factor $k$ is wrongly put inside the logarithm as a multiplier of $(x+2)$, B swaps the roles of $a$ and $k$, and C replaces $x+2$ by $2x$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If matrix $\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&k&2\\2&-6&0\\1&-2&-4\end{pmatrix}$, then the value of $k$ for which $|\mathbf A|=4$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand along the third column $(2,0,-4)$: $|\mathbf A|=2\,C_{13}+(-4)\,C_{33}$, where $C_{13}=+\begin{vmatrix}2&-6\\1&-2\end{vmatrix}=-4+6=2$ and $C_{33}=+\begin{vmatrix}-1&k\\2&-6\end{vmatrix}=6-2k$. Hence $|\mathbf A|=4-4(6-2k)=8k-20$. Setting $8k-20=4$ gives $k=3$. Check: $k=3$ gives $8(3)-20=4$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, where $f(x)=\ln(4+x^2)$, then $f'(2)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: By the chain rule $f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{4+x^2}\cdot 2x=\dfrac{2x}{4+x^2}$. At $x=2$: $f'(2)=\dfrac{4}{4+4}=\dfrac12$. Option A ($\tfrac14$) forgets the factor $2x$ from the chain rule. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The period of the trigonometric function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, where $f(x)=\sin\dfrac23 x$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $\dfrac43\pi$   B) $\dfrac23\pi$   C) $\dfrac34\pi$   D) $\dfrac32\pi$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The function $\sin(bx)$ has period $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$. Here $b=\dfrac23$, so the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{2/3}=3\pi$. None of the four options equals $3\pi$: option A ($\tfrac43\pi$) is the period of $\sin\tfrac32x$, and option D ($\tfrac32\pi$) the period of $\sin\tfrac43x$, so the printed function may have been mistyped. The correct value is therefore missing from the options and the question is left open: **the period is $3\pi$.**



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: If a polynomial $P(x)$ produces a quotient $(x^2+2x+1)$ and a remainder $5$ when divided by $(x+1)$, then $P(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: By the division identity $P(x)=(x+1)\,Q(x)+R$ with $Q(x)=x^2+2x+1=(x+1)^2$ and $R=5$. So $P(x)=(x+1)^3+5=x^3+3x^2+3x+1+5=x^3+3x^2+3x+6$. Check: $P(-1)=-1+3-3+6=5$, the remainder. Options B, C and D change one coefficient (a slip in the product $(x+1)(x^2+2x+1)$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The parametric equations of a curve are $1-x=\tan\theta$ and $[y]=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$. The cartesian equation of this curve is
questions.corrige_markdown: (The symbol $y$ on the left of the second equation is not legible in the scan and is restored in brackets: $y=\sec\theta$, the only reading that gives a cartesian equation in $x$ and $y$.) Use $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$: $y^2=1+(1-x)^2=1+1-2x+x^2=x^2-2x+2$. Hence $x^2-y^2-2x+2=0$. Option A has the wrong sign of $2x$, and B and D have a wrong coefficient of $x$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If the cartesian equation of a plane is $x-2y+z-5=0$, then the vector normal to this plane is

*Options as printed:* A) $\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-\mathbf k$   B) $\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+\mathbf k$   C) $\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-\mathbf k$   D) $\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+\mathbf k$
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a plane $ax+by+cz=d$ the vector $a\mathbf i+b\mathbf j+c\mathbf k$ is normal to the plane. Here $a=1$, $b=-2$, $c=1$, so a normal vector is $\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+\mathbf k$, which is option B. The scan prints options A and C identically ($\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-\mathbf k$), which is why the question is not marked automatically.

**Intended answer: B ($\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+\mathbf k$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Some values of the function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ are given in the table below:

| $x$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $15$ | $28$ | $k$ |

If by the trapezium rule $\displaystyle\int_2^5 f(x)\,dx\approx 68$, then the value of the constant $k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The ordinates are equally spaced with $h=1$ (three strips). The trapezium rule gives $\displaystyle\int_2^5 f\,dx\approx\dfrac h2\left[y_0+y_3+2(y_1+y_2)\right]=\dfrac12\left[5+k+2(15+28)\right]=\dfrac12(91+k)$. Setting $\dfrac12(91+k)=68$ gives $91+k=136$, so $k=45$. Check: $\dfrac12(91+45)=68$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $x_1$ is a first approximate root of the equation $f(x)=0$. By Newton-Raphson's procedure, a second approximate root of this equation is given by
questions.corrige_markdown: The tangent to $y=f(x)$ at $(x_1,f(x_1))$ has equation $y-f(x_1)=f'(x_1)(x-x_1)$. It meets the $x$-axis ($y=0$) where $x=x_1-\dfrac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)}$, and this is the next approximation $x_2$. Options A and B invert the quotient, and B and D use a plus sign, which moves away from the root. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $\mathrm f$ is defined by $\mathrm f(x)=\dfrac{2x-3}{x+1}$, $x\in\mathbb R$, $x\neq-1$, the value of $\mathrm f^{-1}(0)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\mathrm f^{-1}(0)$ is the value of $x$ such that $\mathrm f(x)=0$. $\dfrac{2x-3}{x+1}=0\iff 2x-3=0\iff x=\dfrac32$ (and $x=\tfrac32\neq-1$). Check with the inverse: from $y=\dfrac{2x-3}{x+1}$ we get $x=\dfrac{y+3}{2-y}$, so $\mathrm f^{-1}(0)=\dfrac32$. Option D or C confuse $\mathrm f^{-1}(0)$ with a reciprocal or with $\mathrm f(0)=-3$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ for which the lines $\mathbf r=3\mathbf i-\mathbf j+\mathbf k+\lambda(\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-\mathbf k)$ and $\mathbf r=4\mathbf i+4\mathbf j+\mathbf k+\mu(-\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$ intersect are
questions.corrige_markdown: At an intersection the components are equal. $\mathbf i$: $3+\lambda=4-\mu$. $\mathbf j$: $-1+2\lambda=4+\mu$. $\mathbf k$: $1-\lambda=1+2\mu$. From the $\mathbf k$ equation $\lambda=-2\mu$. Substituting in the $\mathbf i$ equation: $3-2\mu=4-\mu$, so $\mu=-1$ and $\lambda=2$. Check with the $\mathbf j$ equation: $-1+4=3$ and $4+(-1)=3$. The intersection point is $(5,3,-1)$ on both lines. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of ways of arranging $5$ girls on a bench if the two left-handed girls must be together is
questions.corrige_markdown: Treat the two left-handed girls as one block. The block and the other three girls make $4$ objects, which can be arranged in $4!=24$ ways. Within the block the two girls can swap places in $2!=2$ ways. Total: $24\times2=48$. Option A ($24$) forgets the internal order of the block. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\sin\left(x+\dfrac\pi6\right)-\sin\left(x-\dfrac\pi6\right)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\sin A-\sin B=2\cos\dfrac{A+B}{2}\sin\dfrac{A-B}{2}$ with $A=x+\dfrac\pi6$, $B=x-\dfrac\pi6$: $2\cos x\,\sin\dfrac\pi6=2\cos x\cdot\dfrac12=\cos x$. Check by expansion: $\sin x\cos\tfrac\pi6+\cos x\sin\tfrac\pi6-\sin x\cos\tfrac\pi6+\cos x\sin\tfrac\pi6=2\cos x\sin\tfrac\pi6=\cos x$. Options A and D have the wrong sign or the wrong function. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The graph of $y=\dfrac{4}{x^2-1}$ has
questions.corrige_markdown: The denominator $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ vanishes at $x=\pm1$ while the numerator $4$ does not, so there are two vertical asymptotes $x=1$ and $x=-1$. As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{4}{x^2-1}\to0$, so $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote. Option A denies the horizontal asymptote, B lists only one vertical asymptote, and C gives $y=4$, which is the numerator and not the limit. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: two vertical asymptotes $x=\pm1$ and no horizontal asymptote
one vertical asymptote $x=1$ and one horizontal asymptote $y=0$
two vertical asymptotes $x=\pm1$ and a horizontal asymptote $y=4$
two vertical asymptotes $x=\pm1$ and a horizontal asymptote $y=0$

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-2xy=0$. If $y=1$ when $x=1$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Separate the variables: $\dfrac{dy}{y}=2x\,dx$, so $\ln|y|=x^2+C$ and $y=Ae^{x^2}$. The condition $y(1)=1$ gives $1=Ae$, so $A=e^{-1}$ and $y=e^{x^2-1}$. Check: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x\,e^{x^2-1}=2xy$. Option C fails the condition ($y(1)=e$), B gives $y(1)=e^2$, and D satisfies the condition but solves $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2xy$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coefficient of $x^2$ in the binomial expansion of $\left(1+\dfrac12x\right)^{\frac12}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For $(1+u)^{1/2}$ the coefficient of $u^2$ is $\dfrac{\frac12\left(\frac12-1\right)}{2!}=\dfrac{\frac12\cdot\left(-\frac12\right)}{2}=-\dfrac18$. With $u=\dfrac x2$, $u^2=\dfrac{x^2}{4}$, so the coefficient of $x^2$ is $-\dfrac18\times\dfrac14=-\dfrac1{32}$. Option B ($-\tfrac1{16}$) comes from using $u=\tfrac x2$ without squaring the $\tfrac12$. Expansion: $1+\dfrac x4-\dfrac{x^2}{32}+\cdots$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coordinates of the points where the curves $y=2x-3$ and $y=x^2-2x$ intersect are
questions.corrige_markdown: Equate the two expressions: $x^2-2x=2x-3$, so $x^2-4x+3=0$, i.e. $(x-1)(x-3)=0$. Then $x=1$ gives $y=2(1)-3=-1$ and $x=3$ gives $y=2(3)-3=3$. Check on the parabola: $1-2=-1$ and $9-6=3$. The points are $(1,-1)$ and $(3,3)$. Options B and D use a wrong $y$ value for $x=3$ or $x=1$, and C has the wrong sign of the first point. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of the constant $k$ for which $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac{[k]}{2^{r-1}}\right)=10$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: (The scan prints the general term as $\dfrac{1}{2^{r-1}}$ with no constant $k$, although the question asks for $k$; the numerator $k$ is restored in brackets. Without $k$ the printed series sums to $2$, never $10$.) The series $k\left(1+\dfrac12+\dfrac14+\cdots\right)$ is geometric with first term $k$ and common ratio $\dfrac12$, so $|r|<1$ and the sum to infinity is $\dfrac{k}{1-\frac12}=2k$. Setting $2k=10$ gives $k=5$. Option C ($2$) is the sum of the series when $k=1$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If a linear reduction of the relationship $y=ax^n$ produced the result $\log y=2\log x+1.3$, then the approximate values of $a$ and $n$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Taking logarithms of $y=ax^n$ gives $\log y=n\log x+\log a$. Comparing with $\log y=2\log x+1.3$: $n=2$ (the gradient) and $\log a=1.3$ (the intercept). With common logarithms (base $10$), $a=10^{1.3}\approx19.95\approx20$. So $a\approx20$ and $n=2$. Options A and C use $a=2$ (reading the intercept $1.3$ as $a$ rounded), and C and D use $n=20$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The complex number $z$, in the form $a+bi$, for which $(1-2i)z=3-i$ is
The value of $a$ for which the quadratic equation $2x^2-6x+3a=0$ has equal roots is
questions.corrige_markdown: Equal roots require the discriminant to be zero: $b^2-4ac=(-6)^2-4(2)(3a)=36-24a=0$, so $a=\dfrac{36}{24}=\dfrac32$. Check: $2x^2-6x+\dfrac92=2\left(x-\dfrac32\right)^2$, which has the double root $x=\dfrac32$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{x}{1+2x^2}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $\dfrac d{dx}(1+2x^2)=4x$, $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{1+2x^2}\,dx=\dfrac14\ln(1+2x^2)$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{x}{1+2x^2}\,dx=\dfrac14\left[\ln9-\ln3\right]=\dfrac14\ln\dfrac93=\dfrac14\ln3$. Option C ($2\ln 3$) or A ($4\ln 3$) misplace the factor $\tfrac14$, and B ($\tfrac12\ln3$) comes from using $\tfrac12\ln$ instead of $\tfrac14\ln$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: MECHANICS**

A particle has position vector $\mathbf r$ at time $t$ seconds given by $\mathbf r=\left(e^{2t}\mathbf i+e^{3t}\mathbf j\right)$ m. The velocity and acceleration of the particle when $t=0$ are respectively
questions.corrige_markdown: Velocity: $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=\left(2e^{2t}\mathbf i+3e^{3t}\mathbf j\right)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so at $t=0$ ($e^0=1$): $\mathbf v=(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Acceleration: $\mathbf a=\dfrac{d\mathbf v}{dt}=\left(4e^{2t}\mathbf i+9e^{3t}\mathbf j\right)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so at $t=0$: $\mathbf a=(4\mathbf i+9\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Option C swaps the components of the velocity, and B and D carry a wrong sign. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is projected from a point on a horizontal plane with speed $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at an angle $30^\circ$ to the plane. The horizontal range $R$ covered by the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown: The value of $g$ is not printed in this question; $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is used, as in Questions 47 and 48. Vertical motion: the particle returns to the plane when $0=(10\sin30^\circ)t-\tfrac12(10)t^2$, i.e. $t=\dfrac{2\times5}{10}=1\ \mathrm s$. Horizontal motion at constant speed $10\cos30^\circ=5\sqrt3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives $R=5\sqrt3\times1=5\sqrt3\ \mathrm m\approx8.66\ \mathrm m$. Equivalently $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\alpha}{g}=\dfrac{100\sin60^\circ}{10}=5\sqrt3$. (With $g=9.8$ the range would be $8.84\ \mathrm m$, which matches no option, so $g=10$ is the intended value.) **Answer: C.**

themes: elastic strings and potential energy mechanics
questions.enonce_markdown: When the length of a spring is $60\%$ of its natural length, the thrust in the spring is $10\ \mathrm N$, the modulus of elasticity of the spring is
questions.corrige_markdown: Let the natural length be $l$ and the modulus $\lambda$. The spring is compressed to $0.6\,l$, so its compression is $x=0.4\,l$. Hooke's law for a spring: $T=\dfrac{\lambda x}{l}=\dfrac{\lambda(0.4\,l)}{l}=0.4\lambda$. Setting $0.4\lambda=10$ gives $\lambda=25\ \mathrm N$. Option A ($\tfrac{50}{3}$) results from taking the compression as $0.6\,l$ ($\lambda=10/0.6$), and D ($4$) from multiplying $10$ by $0.4$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A centripetal force of $72\ \mathrm N$ causes a particle of mass $4\ \mathrm{kg}$ to move in a horizontal circle of radius $2\ \mathrm m$. The angular speed of the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown: The centripetal force is $F=m\omega^2r$. So $72=4\,\omega^2(2)=8\omega^2$, giving $\omega^2=9$ and $\omega=3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. (The linear speed is $v=\omega r=6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, not asked.) Option A gives $\omega^2$ instead of $\omega$, and C and D are in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, units of linear speed, not of angular speed. **Answer: B.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown: Two particles of masses $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ are placed at the points $(3,1)$ and $(8,6)$ respectively. The position of their center of mass is at the point
questions.corrige_markdown: The centre of mass of particles is $\bar x=\dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}$ and $\bar y=\dfrac{\sum m_iy_i}{\sum m_i}$. $\bar x=\dfrac{2(3)+3(8)}{5}=\dfrac{30}{5}=6$ and $\bar y=\dfrac{2(1)+3(6)}{5}=\dfrac{20}{5}=4$. The centre of mass is $(6,4)$, nearer to the heavier particle. Option B $(5.5,3.5)$ is the unweighted midpoint. **Answer: A.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown:
Fig. 1 shows a uniform sheet of metal in the form of letter L with dimensions in metres.

![fig-1](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

The distance of its center of mass from edge $AB$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Reading Fig. 1: $AB$ is the vertical left edge of the L (length $6\ \mathrm m$, $B$ at the top, $A$ at the bottom), the upright arm is $2\ \mathrm m$ wide, and the foot of the L is $6\ \mathrm m$ long and $2\ \mathrm m$ high. Take distances $x$ from the edge $AB$. Split the sheet into the upright arm ($2\ \mathrm m$ by $6\ \mathrm m$) and the part of the foot to the right of it ($4\ \mathrm m$ by $2\ \mathrm m$). The sheet is uniform, so masses are proportional to areas.

| Part | Area ($\mathrm m^2$) | Distance of its centre from $AB$ ($\mathrm m$) |
|---|---|---|
| Upright arm | $2\times6=12$ | $1$ |
| Right part of the foot | $4\times2=8$ | $2+2=4$ |

$\bar x=\dfrac{12(1)+8(4)}{12+8}=\dfrac{44}{20}=2.2\ \mathrm m$. (By the symmetry of the L about its diagonal the distance from the bottom edge is the same.) Option D ($2.5$) is the unweighted mean of $1$ and $4$, and C ($3$) is the centre of the $6\ \mathrm m$ by $6\ \mathrm m$ square. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A uniform ladder $AB$, of length $2a$, rests in limiting equilibrium with its top end against a rough vertical wall and its lower end on a rough horizontal floor. The forces acting on the ladder are as shown in fig. 2 below.

![fig-2](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

The angle $\theta$ which $AB$ makes with the floor is given by

*Options as printed:* A) $\tan\theta=\dfrac35$   B) $\tan\theta=\dfrac53$   C) $\sin\theta=\dfrac35$ [as printed]   D) $\sin\theta=\dfrac35$ [as printed]
questions.corrige_markdown:
Reading Fig. 2 (wall on the left, $B$ the top end): at $B$ the wall exerts a normal reaction $9\ \mathrm N$ (horizontal, away from the wall) and a frictional force $6\ \mathrm N$ upwards; the weight is $42\ \mathrm N$ downwards at the midpoint of $AB$; at $A$ the floor exerts a normal reaction $36\ \mathrm N$ upwards and a frictional force $9\ \mathrm N$ towards the wall. Check of resolution: vertically $6+36=42$ and horizontally $9=9$. Take moments about $A$ (a point through which the $36\ \mathrm N$ and $9\ \mathrm N$ forces at $A$ have no moment). The horizontal distance from $A$ to the weight is $a\cos\theta$ and to $B$ is $2a\cos\theta$; the height of $B$ is $2a\sin\theta$. The moment of the weight about $A$ is balanced by the moments of the two forces at $B$ (the $6\ \mathrm N$ force acts at horizontal distance $2a\cos\theta$ from $A$ and the $9\ \mathrm N$ force at height $2a\sin\theta$ above $A$): $42\,(a\cos\theta)=6\,(2a\cos\theta)+9\,(2a\sin\theta)$. Divide by $a$: $42\cos\theta=12\cos\theta+18\sin\theta$, so $30\cos\theta=18\sin\theta$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{30}{18}=\dfrac53$ (so $\theta\approx59^\circ$). Option B is the only option equal to $\tan\theta=\dfrac53$. The scan prints options C and D identically ($\sin\theta=\dfrac35$), with overprinted fractions, which is why the question is not marked automatically.

**Intended answer: B ($\tan\theta=\dfrac53$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A girl on a ship, whose velocity is $(4\mathbf i-7\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is watching a boat whose velocity is $(-8\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The speed of the boat as it appears to the girl on the ship is
questions.corrige_markdown: The velocity of the boat relative to the girl is ${}_B\mathbf v_G=\mathbf v_B-\mathbf v_G=(-8\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)-(4\mathbf i-7\mathbf j)=(-12\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Its magnitude (the speed) is $\sqrt{(-12)^2+5^2}=\sqrt{169}=13\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Options A and B are velocity vectors, not a speed (B is the velocity of the girl relative to the boat), and D has no meaning (the magnitudes cannot be subtracted). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle accelerating from rest has its speed $v\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at time $t$ seconds given by $v=6t-\dfrac12t^2$. The acceleration of the particle when $v=10$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The acceleration is $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=6-t$. When $v=10$: $6t-\tfrac12t^2=10$, i.e. $t^2-12t+20=0$, so $(t-2)(t-10)=0$ and $t=2$ or $t=10$. The speed rises until $t=6$ (where $a=0$ and $v=18$) and then falls, so $v=10$ happens twice. The particle is described as accelerating, so $t=2\ \mathrm s$ and $a=6-2=4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. (At the second time, $t=10$, $a=-4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which has the same magnitude $4$.) Option C ($2$) is the time $t$, not the acceleration. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A smooth sphere $A$ of mass $4\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ collides directly with a smooth sphere $B$ of mass $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction. Given that the speed of $A$ after impact is $0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the kinetic energy of $B$ after impact is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take the initial direction of $A$ as positive. Conservation of momentum: $4(5)+3(-4)=4v_A+3v_B$, so $8=4v_A+3v_B$. If $A$ keeps moving in its original direction, $v_A=0.5$ and $3v_B=8-2=6$, so $v_B=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The kinetic energy of $B$ is $\tfrac12(3)(2)^2=6\ \mathrm J$. (Coefficient of restitution $e=\dfrac{2-0.5}{5+4}=\dfrac16$, which is allowed.) Option A ($24$ J) is the kinetic energy of $B$ before impact, $\tfrac12(3)(4)^2$, and D ($6.5$ J) is the kinetic energy of both spheres after impact, $0.5+6$. Remark: the sentence gives only the speed of $A$, not its direction; if $A$ rebounded ($v_A=-0.5$), $v_B=\tfrac{10}{3}$ and the energy would be $\tfrac{50}{3}\approx16.7\ \mathrm J$, which is not an option, so the option set confirms the first reading. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The work done by a force $\mathbf F=(\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-4\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ which moves its point of application from a point $A$ with position vector $\mathbf r_A=(3\mathbf i-4\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$ to another point $B$ with position vector $\mathbf r_B=(-\mathbf i+6\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $47\ \mathrm J$   B) $-35\ \mathrm J$   C) $-15\ \mathrm J$   D) $35\ \mathrm J$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The displacement is $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A=(-\mathbf i+6\mathbf k)-(3\mathbf i-4\mathbf k)=(-4\mathbf i+10\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$. The work done is the scalar product $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=(1)(-4)+(-2)(0)+(-4)(10)=-4-40=-44\ \mathrm J$. This value is in none of the four options ($47$, $-35$, $-15$, $35$), so the question is left open: **the work done is $-44\ \mathrm J$** (negative because the force has a component opposite to the displacement).



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance
questions.enonce_markdown: The engine of a car of mass $1{,}200\ \mathrm{kg}$ works at a constant rate of $54\ \mathrm{kW}$ up a road inclined at an angle $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac15\right)$ to the horizontal. Given that the non-gravitational resistance to the motion of the car is $300\ \mathrm N$ and taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the maximum speed of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown: At maximum speed the acceleration is zero, so along the road the driving force $F$ balances the resistance plus the component of the weight down the slope: $F=300+mg\sin\alpha=300+1200(10)\left(\dfrac15\right)=300+2400=2700\ \mathrm N$. The power is $P=Fv$, so $v=\dfrac{P}{F}=\dfrac{54000}{2700}=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Option C or D come from using only part of the forces (for instance $54000/300=180$ ignores the weight). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A block of mass $4\ \mathrm{kg}$ slides down a rough plane inclined at $30$ to the horizontal at constant speed. The block covers a distance $0.8\ \mathrm m$. Taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the work done against friction is
questions.corrige_markdown: At constant speed the net force along the plane is zero, so the friction force equals the component of the weight down the plane: $F=mg\sin30^\circ=4(10)\left(\dfrac12\right)=20\ \mathrm N$. The work done against friction over $0.8\ \mathrm m$ is $W=F\,d=20\times0.8=16\ \mathrm J$ (equal to the loss of gravitational potential energy $mgh=4(10)(0.8\sin30^\circ)=16\ \mathrm J$). Options A and D are in kJ, a factor $1000$ too large, and C ($32$ J) is double. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: From a speed of $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, a car decelerates uniformly to rest, covering a distance of $80\ \mathrm m$. The deceleration of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $v^2=u^2+2as$ with $u=20$, $v=0$, $s=80$: $0=400+2a(80)$, so $a=-\dfrac{400}{160}=-\dfrac52\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The acceleration is $-\dfrac52\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so the deceleration (the magnitude of the retardation) is $\dfrac52\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Check: $t=\dfrac{20}{2.5}=8\ \mathrm s$ and $s=\dfrac{20+0}{2}\times8=80\ \mathrm m$. Option A is the acceleration, which carries the minus sign; the deceleration asked for is positive. Remark: options A and B differ only by sign, and some markers accept the signed value for 'deceleration', so the intended key may be A; the strict meaning of deceleration gives B. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two dice are thrown together. The probability of having at least a SIX is
questions.corrige_markdown: Use the complement: $P(\text{no six})=\dfrac56\times\dfrac56=\dfrac{25}{36}$, so $P(\text{at least one six})=1-\dfrac{25}{36}=\dfrac{11}{36}$. Check by counting: $36$ equally likely outcomes, of which $6+6-1=11$ contain at least one six. Option B and C count only one or two of the favourable outcomes. **Answer: A.**
